title: Movable-type periphery: reusable pre-tested sense/decoder tiles across array generations
idea: Like Gutenberg's reusable type sorts, cast a library of periphery tiles (sense-amp strips, sub-wordline driver strips, pump and I/O tiles) on a depreciated logic wafer, test them, and hybrid-bond known-good tiles under each new array die. When the array shrinks, only a thin bitline-pitch adapter layer is re-cut; the tile library is reused for 3-4 array generations.
why: Periphery (~49% of die) is redesigned and re-fabbed on the expensive DRAM node every generation; reusable tiles cut DRAM-node wafer area per bit ~35-45% and periphery mask/NRE cost ~70%.

title: Jacquard warp-weft coincident wordline selection replaces tree decoders
idea: Borrow the Jacquard loom, where a hook lifts only where card and lifting bar coincide: each sub-wordline driver is a two-input threshold switch at the crossing of a 'warp' line (high address bits, sqrt(N) lines) and a 'weft' line (low bits, sqrt(N) lines). Each line supplies only half the boost charge, so half-selected drivers stay below threshold and only the doubly-selected wordline fires.
why: Cuts decoder transistors per wordline from ~6-10 to ~2 and predecode routing from O(log N) tracks per row to O(sqrt N) per mat: ~40-60% row-decoder area reduction.

title: Miura-fold bitlines: true and complement stacked vertically, not side by side
idea: Fold the bitline pair like Miura-ori: the true bitline runs on tier 1 and its complement directly above on tier 2, swapping tiers every 64 cells through a zig-zag via 'crease'. Both lines see identical wordline and neighbor coupling, giving folded-bitline noise rejection in the lateral footprint of an open bitline.
why: Open-bitline cell density with folded-bitline common-mode immunity, and each sense amp gets 2x the lateral pitch; ~30% less signal margin needed and an easier SA-pitch wall.

title: Block-copolymer self-assembled gates for near-zero-LER sense-amp transistors
idea: Define only the sense-amp input-pair gates with directed self-assembly of a lamellar block copolymer guided by a coarse litho trench; the molecularly set period gives ~1 nm line-edge roughness instead of ~2-3 nm from resist. Both transistors of a pair are cut from the same lamella so they share edge statistics.
why: SA offset sets the minimum bitline signal; halving LER-driven mismatch cuts required signal ~30%, allowing ~1.4x longer bitlines (fewer SA strips, ~8-10% die) or a smaller capacitor.

title: Splat-quenched metallic-glass gates kill grain-driven sense-amp mismatch
idea: Borrow rapid-quench casting of metallic glass: deposit the SA gate metal as an amorphous alloy (e.g., Ta-Si-N or Zr-Cu-Al sputtered on a cold substrate) with no grains. With no random TiN grain orientations there is no grain work-function variation between the two latch transistors.
why: Work-function variation is a leading Vt-mismatch source in high-k metal-gate periphery; removing it cuts SA offset sigma ~30-40%, so bitline signal (and Cs or VARY) can drop ~25-35%.

title: Perfecting-press wafer: periphery printed on the backside of the array
idea: Like a perfecting press that prints both sides of a sheet in one pass, thin the finished array wafer to ~1 um and build low-temperature periphery transistors (laser-annealed Si or oxide FETs) on its backside. These connect to bitlines and wordlines through sub-um nano-TSVs directly beneath each mat.
why: Periphery stops consuming front-side area: array efficiency rises from ~51% to ~85%, ~1.6x bits per wafer without a litho shrink, and SA-to-bitline paths get shorter.

title: Xerographic bitlines: light-switched photoconductive segments shorten bitlines on demand
idea: Borrow the photocopier drum: build each bitline from segments joined by amorphous-silicon photoconductor bridges that insulate in the dark. An on-chip SiN waveguide fed by an off-chip laser lights only the bridges between the accessed segment and the SA, so the SA sees a short, low-capacitance line and the rest is electrically absent.
why: Bitline capacitance per access falls 4-8x, multiplying the signal: Cs could drop from ~5 fF to ~1-2 fF (breaking the charge wall), with one SA serving very long bitlines.

title: Braided trio bitlines with permutation-coded, reference-free sensing
idea: Like a three-strand braid, route three bitlines that rotate positions every few cells so all see identical coupling. Store data as the rank order of three distinct charge levels across three cells (6 permutations = 2.58 bits per 3 cells) and read it with three pairwise comparators and no mid-rail reference.
why: Common-mode leakage shifts all three cells together, so rank order survives ~2-4x longer: refresh power drops and reference-generation circuits leave the periphery, at a ~14% raw density cost.

title: Hydraulic-accumulator antiferroelectric reservoirs replace oversized wordline charge pumps
idea: Like a hydraulic accumulator that banks pressure for peak demand, put antiferroelectric ZrO2 capacitors under the sub-wordline driver strips. A small pump charges them slowly, and during activate bursts they release a large charge at a near-constant voltage plateau set by the field-induced phase switch-back.
why: VPP pumps are sized for tFAW peak bursts; AFE energy density is ~5-10x MOS caps and its plateau self-regulates, shrinking pump + decap area ~50-70% (several % of die) and cutting pump losses.

title: Photographic-development tunnel-diode latch amplifies latent bitline charge
idea: Borrow film development, which amplifies a latent image of a few silver atoms by ~10^9: place a Goto pair of Esaki tunnel diodes on each bitline pair, biased near the peak of its N-shaped I-V. A few millivolts of cell signal tips it into one valley state in picoseconds, and a CMOS restore stage follows.
why: NDR latch offset is set by junction doping, not gate litho, and it switches at ~0.3-0.5 V: ~3x smaller usable bitline signal and lower array voltage, attacking both the charge wall and the CV^2 voltage floor.

title: Andon-cord sense amps flag slow-resolving cells for targeted refresh
idea: Like Toyota's andon cord, which any worker pulls to flag a problem, each SA strip gets a tiny resolution-time detector (XOR of the latch nodes sampled at a fixed delay after enable). Any SA still metastable at the strobe pulls a shared andon line, so the controller logs that row as weak and refreshes it more often while others refresh less.
why: Finds weak, leaky cells during normal traffic with no test overhead; most rows can run 4-8x longer refresh intervals, cutting refresh energy (~46 fJ/bit) and bandwidth loss ~60-75%.

title: Spinning-jenny sensing: one amplifier spins across sixteen gain-cell bitlines
idea: As one spinning-jenny wheel drove many spindles, pair non-destructive-read gain cells with one shared, high-quality sense amp per 16 read bitlines through a 1:16 mux. Reads do not destroy data, so only requested columns are sensed and no row restore is needed.
why: SA count drops 16x (SA area from ~15-20% of die to ~2%) and the 128x page overfetch disappears (~5.9 pJ per useful bit toward <1 pJ).

title: Ink-jet drop-on-demand cells: double-gated access opens one cell only
idea: Like a drop-on-demand print head that fires only the nozzles needed, give each access transistor two gates: a row gate (wordline) and an orthogonal column gate (column-select line). A cell conducts only at the row-AND-column intersection, so a 64-bit burst opens 64 cells and fires 64 SAs instead of 8,192.
why: Removes the 128x overfetch and the restore of untouched cells: ~50-100x less activate energy per useful bit, and row hammer weakens because full rows are never activated.

title: Progressive-die cascade: three charge-transfer stages pre-amplify before latching
idea: Like a progressive stamping die that forms a part through several small stations, pass the bitline charge through three cascaded switched-capacitor charge-transfer stages, each dumping charge from a larger capacitor onto one ~3x smaller. The result is ~20-27x voltage gain before a relaxed latch fires.
why: A large signal at the latch tolerates small, high-offset SA devices (SA area ~-40%) and lets bitlines carry 2-3x more cells, or allows Cs to fall ~2x toward 2-3 fF.

title: Flying-shuttle sense enable rides the wordline's RC wave
idea: Like Kay's flying shuttle carrying the weft across every warp in one throw, route sense-enable on a delay-matched line parallel to the wordline. Each SA then fires just after its own cell's wordline actually rises, instead of every SA waiting for the slowest far-end cell.
why: Removes worst-case wordline-RC margin from tRCD (~2-4 ns of ~14 ns, ~20% faster activate) and allows 2x longer wordlines, so half as many sub-wordline driver strips (~5% die).

title: Felted random-network decoder, mapped after manufacture
idea: Like felt made by matting random fibers instead of weaving, spray a sparse random network of nanowire switches between a few predecode lines and the wordline ends. Post-fab test discovers which address code reaches which wordline and stores the map in a small table, so no lithographically defined decoder is needed at wordline pitch.
why: Decoders for 3D-DRAM tiers and fine-pitch arrays are costly to pattern; a stochastic decoder needs no critical litho, cutting decoder area and masks ~50-80% for vertical stacks.

title: Continuous-casting sensing: no precharge, sense against the previous state
idea: Like continuous casting that never stops to pour a new ingot, bitlines are never equalized to VDD/2: they keep the last row's resolved values. The SA chooses between two references (VDD-delta or delta) based on the bitline's held previous bit, so the next activate starts at once.
why: Removes tRP (~14 ns) and equalize/precharge energy (~20-30% of activate energy), raising effective random-access bandwidth ~15-25%.

title: Dairy-cooperative periphery foundry co-owned by rival DRAM makers
idea: Like farmer co-ops that share one creamery, DRAM vendors jointly own a U.S. fab that makes only periphery/CMOS-under-array logic wafers to a common bond interface. Each vendor bonds its proprietary array wafers on top and buys periphery at cost.
why: Pools capex for the ~49%-of-die periphery function, frees each vendor's DRAM-node capacity for cells (~1.5x bits per DRAM wafer), and puts a large memory fab in the U.S.

title: Permanent-mold sense amps: ferroelectric gate nulls each amplifier's offset forever
idea: Like a permanent metal mold that is set once and reused for thousands of castings, give one transistor of each SA input pair an HZO ferroelectric gate layer. At wafer test a binary search programs its polarization to cancel that SA's measured offset, and it stays trimmed for life with no fuse area.
why: Residual offset falls from ~15-20 mV sigma to ~3-5 mV, so bitline signal can drop ~3x: 2-3x longer bitlines (SA strip area -50%) or Cs reduced to ~2 fF.

title: Pop-up-book sense amplifier: vertical-channel latch fits bitline pitch
idea: Like a pop-up book that stands flat art upright, build the SA cross-coupled pair and equalizer from vertical-channel transistors in a two-tier stack (n-latch below, p-latch above). One complete SA then fits under a single 2F bitline pitch instead of a 4-6F-wide strip.
why: Shrinks SA-strip footprint ~3-4x (SA strips are ~10-15% of die) and enables open-bitline 4F^2 arrays without an SA-pitch crisis.

title: Flemish-bond stacking: staggered tiers share each sense-amp strip vertically
idea: Like bricks laid in Flemish bond so joints never line up, offset alternate 3D-DRAM tiers by half a mat. Every SA strip then sits between the bitline ends of the tier above and the tier below and serves both through short vertical vias.
why: Halves SA strips per bit in 3D DRAM, attacking the periphery overhead behind the ~26-tier break-even; break-even tier count could fall ~20-30%.

title: Pin-factory split: tiny per-pair preamps, shared high-voltage restore drivers
idea: Adam Smith's pin factory split one job into specialized steps: split the SA into a minimal thin-oxide preamp per bitline pair that only decides and holds the bit, plus one strong restore driver shared by four pairs. The shared driver writes full-swing values back in four ~3 ns phases within tRAS.
why: Restore devices are the largest part of the SA; sharing them 4:1 cuts SA-strip area ~30-40% and lets the preamp use smaller, better-matched devices.

title: Fractional-distillation sensing: one timed comparator reads multi-level cells
idea: Like a distillation column where each fraction boils off at its own temperature, each 2T gain cell's stored level sets how fast its read bitline discharges, and a single comparator timestamps the threshold crossing. Early/mid/late/no crossing yields 2 bits per cell from one comparator and a shared counter instead of three SAs per bitline.
why: Enables 2-bit/cell DRAM-class arrays (2x density) without tripling SA area; sensing periphery per bit roughly halves.

title: Fluidic self-assembly drops 180 nm periphery blocks into array wafers
idea: Borrow 1990s fluidic self-assembly (Alien Technology, 1994): make charge pumps, I/O, fuse/test and command logic as trapezoidal ~50 um blocks on depreciated 180 nm lines. Pour them as a slurry over the array wafer, whose etched recesses accept only the matching shape, then wire them with one coarse i-line metal layer.
why: Moves the ~20-25% of die that is not pitch-matched periphery off the leading-edge wafer onto ~$600 200 mm wafers made in U.S. fabs: ~25% more bits per expensive wafer and more U.S. content.

title: LCD-line excimer laser crystallizes poly-Si periphery above the array
idea: Borrow the 1990s LTPS LCD backplane process: deposit a-Si over the finished array, then crystallize it with excimer-laser pulses that melt only the top ~50 nm while the array stays below ~400 C. Build 180 nm-rule periphery (pumps, predecoders, control) in that layer and wire it down to the array.
why: Periphery-over-array with legacy tools reclaims ~30-40% of die area; LTPS mobility (~100-300 cm^2/Vs) is enough for logic that does not need to match bitline pitch.

title: Burn-in tempering: stress each sense amp until its offset vanishes
idea: Like tempering steel with controlled heat, use the 1990s wafer-level burn-in oven to apply asymmetric hot-carrier stress to the stronger transistor of each SA pair, chosen by a built-in offset measurement. The stress shifts its Vt until the pair matches, and the trapped charge makes the shift permanent.
why: SA offset sigma drops ~2-3x with zero added area, allowing ~2x more cells per bitline (SA strips -50% of their ~12% die share) using only legacy burn-in equipment.

title: Anodized-aluminum pore forests become dense charge-pump capacitors
idea: Borrow the architectural-aluminum anodizing line: anodize a sputtered Al layer over the periphery so it self-assembles hexagonal pores ~150 nm wide and 2-3 um deep. Line the pores with a CVD TiN/Ta2O5/TiN stack (a 1990s DRAM capacitor stack) to make 3D capacitors stacked above the pump and decoupling circuits.
why: ~100-200 fF/um^2 vs ~10-20 fF/um^2 for MOS caps: VPP/VBB pump and decap area (several % of die) shrinks ~5-10x using only a wet bench and CVD.

title: Diffusion-furnace bipolar sense amps: BiCMOS revival for millivolt signals
idea: Like a batch furnace that dopes thousands of wafers identically, bipolar transistors match by diffusion depth and emitter area rather than gate litho. Use 1990s BiCMOS to put bipolar differential pre-amps (Vbe mismatch ~0.5 mV) ahead of CMOS latches, shared across column groups.
why: ~10x lower offset than MOS pairs lets bitlines carry 4-8x more cells, or lets a ~1 fF planar capacitor work, so a 180 nm U.S. fab could make dense-enough memory without deep trenches.

title: Camcorder-CCD row buffer: charge packets shuffle to few amplifiers
idea: Borrow the 1990s CCD imager: on activate, every bitline's charge is dumped into a buried-channel CCD register under the SA strip, which holds the row in the charge domain. Only the requested columns are clocked a few stages to floating-diffusion amplifiers with correlated double sampling, then the packets are shifted back to restore.
why: One low-noise amplifier per 8-16 columns instead of one SA per column (SA area -80%); correlated double sampling resolves ~1,000-electron packets, so tiny planar capacitors made at 180 nm can be read.

title: Pre-printed forms: sea-of-gates periphery personalized by two i-line metal masks
idea: Like printers who stock pre-printed letterhead and add only the name, fab one universal 180 nm periphery master with gate-array sites for pumps, decoders and control. Interface width, protocol (DDR/LPDDR/CXL-lite) and redundancy are personalized with just two metal masks, the 1990s ASIC gate-array method.
why: Cuts per-variant mask sets and NRE ~80-90%, so small U.S. fabs can serve many memory SKUs from one wafer inventory.

title: Darkroom dodge-and-burn: per-mat precharge level trimmed at test
idea: Like a printer dodging and burning areas of a photograph, measure each mat's '0' and '1' bitline signal distributions at wafer sort. Then program a 4-bit offset on that mat's precharge voltage with 1990s laser-fuse repair tools, so the reference sits midway between the real, leakage-skewed distributions.
why: Leakage pulls stored '1's down asymmetrically; re-centering recovers ~20-30% of margin, which becomes ~1.5-2x longer refresh intervals or a smaller capacitor.

title: Dropped-stitch knitting: token-chained subarrays replace fuse-compare redundancy
idea: Like a knitter passing over a dropped stitch, a token threads through every subarray at power-up (the Catt-spiral idea from 1989 Anamartic wafer-scale memory). A subarray that fails its built-in self-test simply passes the token on, so the chain itself builds the address map with no fuse banks or address comparators.
why: Removes most fuse arrays and redundancy comparators (~3-6% of die) and gives coarse subarray sparing that tolerates clustered defects, raising yield at 180 nm and above.

title: Fruit-grading line: laser-fused refresh classes per mat
idea: Like a fruit packing line that grades every piece into bins, measure each mat's retention at wafer sort and blow two laser fuses that set its refresh multiplier (1x/2x/4x/8x). The on-die refresh counter then skips cycles for long-retention mats.
why: Most mats retain 4-8x longer than the worst one; refresh energy and bandwidth loss fall ~60-70% for two fuses per mat on 1990s laser repair tools.

title: Die-bank build-to-order: array dies stockpiled, 180 nm interface die added later
idea: Like Dell's build-to-order line, makers stockpile bare array dies (cells and SAs only). A U.S. assembler flip-chips each onto a 180 nm interface/periphery die chosen per customer (DDR, LPDDR, CXL, custom AI) when orders arrive, using 1990s C4 solder bumps and wide, slow buses.
why: Decouples scarce array capacity from interface churn, cuts inventory write-downs, and moves about a third of the memory value-add into U.S. mature fabs.

title: Plywood veneer: Smart-Cut array laminates share one periphery base
idea: Like plywood glued from thin veneers, transfer thin 180 nm array layers (cells and bitline selects only, no periphery) one at a time onto a periphery base wafer using 1995 Smart-Cut hydrogen splitting and oxide bonding. Each veneer's bitlines drop through vertical vias to the shared SA/decoder base.
why: Periphery is built once for 8-16 layers, so array efficiency nears 90% and density scales with layer count instead of lithography: a U.S. 200 mm-fab path to dense memory.

title: Lost-foam casting: sacrificial polymer evaporates into bitline air gaps
idea: Like lost-foam casting, where the foam pattern vaporizes as metal fills the mold, fill between bitlines with a thermally decomposable polynorbornene (late-1990s chemistry) and cap it with porous oxide. A ~425 C bake makes the polymer diffuse out, leaving air gaps.
why: Cuts bitline-to-bitline capacitance ~40% and total bitline capacitance ~20-30%: ~1.3x more signal (fewer SA strips, ~3-4% die) or a ~25% smaller capacitor.

title: Line-shaft wordline boost: one resonant tank powers every subarray
idea: Like a mill's line shaft driving every machine through belts, replace dozens of local VPP charge pumps with one package-level LC resonator (off-chip inductor plus on-chip capacitance). Its ~3 V sinusoid is tapped by bootstrap rectifiers at each sub-wordline driver strip, all built in 180 nm.
why: Local pumps waste ~60-70% of their energy and take ~3-5% of die; resonant delivery recycles wordline charge, cutting VPP energy ~2x and pump area ~70%.

title: Sourdough mother-culture: reference cells that age exactly like data
idea: Like a baker feeding a starter alongside every batch, each mat keeps two reference columns that are rewritten to '1' and '0' at every refresh. On activate they charge-share into a reference that has leaked exactly as much as the data cells since their last refresh.
why: A self-tracking reference removes temperature and time drift and recovers ~20% margin near the end of the refresh window (~1.5x longer refresh) with simple 180 nm circuitry.

title: Core-rope weaving: diode-matrix row decoder with no PMOS
idea: Like Apollo's core-rope memory, where each wire threaded through or around a core encoded a bit, encode each wordline's address by placing or omitting a Schottky diode where it crosses the predecoded lines (one implant mask at 180 nm). The result is a dynamic diode-AND decoder.
why: Diodes are ~4x smaller than a CMOS NAND stack and need no well spacing: decoder area -50-60%, buildable at i-line rules.

title: Selective assembly: pick the best-matched transistor fingers per sense amp
idea: As engine plants pair pistons with bores by measured size, build each SA input side from four half-width candidate fingers. At test, e-fuse switches keep the finger pair whose Vts match best, the way 1990s analog chips trimmed matched pairs.
why: Best-of-4x4 selection cuts offset sigma ~2-3x without advanced litho, so bitlines can double in length; net SA area falls ~20-30% even at 180 nm.

title: Kiln witness cones: in-array cells integrate activation heat-work for row hammer
idea: Like pyrometric cones that slump after enough cumulative kiln heat, each row has a witness cell that gets a small charge kick through a weak device on every activation and leaks it away over time. Refresh reads the witness column and schedules neighbor refresh wherever a witness has slumped past threshold.
why: Replaces megabits of SRAM row-hammer counters in periphery with ~0.1% extra array cells; analog decay tracks hammer physics at ~1k-activation thresholds.

title: Cold forging: 77 K-operated 180 nm DRAM with planar capacitors
idea: Like cold forging, which gains strength by working metal cold, run a 180 nm planar-capacitor DRAM in liquid nitrogen. Junction and subthreshold leakage fall by >10^6 and SA transistors gain ~2x transconductance with lower noise, so small ~2-3 fF planar caps sense reliably and refresh nearly disappears.
why: No tall capacitors, EUV or refresh for a datacenter memory tier on cheap U.S. 180 nm wafers; this offsets part of the ~10x density penalty and cooling cost, and SA area shrinks from better gm and matching.

title: Hydroforming wordlines: bootstrapped local boost replaces high-voltage drivers
idea: Like hydroforming, which shapes metal with uniform fluid pressure instead of heavy punches, precharge each local wordline to VDD through a small thin-oxide device, float it, then pressurize it to ~3 V by capacitive coupling from a shared boost line. This revives the 1970s NMOS bootstrap, so no thick-oxide PMOS is needed at every wordline.
why: Sub-wordline driver strips (~8-10% of die) shrink ~40% because the thick-oxide PMOS and well spacing go away; works with 180 nm devices.

title: Putting-out system: 180 nm module hub does ECC, repair and refresh
idea: Like the pre-industrial putting-out system that sent specialized steps out to cottages, strip on-die ECC, repair maps, refresh scheduling and row-hammer tracking off every DRAM die. Put them in one 180 nm hub chip per module that runs wide and slow (e.g., 512 bits at 400 MHz).
why: On-die ECC and control logic take ~8-12% of die area; one hub per 8-16 dies removes that from every leading-edge die and adds U.S.-made content.

title: Springfield Armory standard: public-domain 180 nm periphery masks for U.S. fabs
idea: Like the Springfield Armory's government-owned gauges that made interchangeable parts possible, a federal program funds and publishes an open periphery reference design, bump map and mask set at 180 nm. Any U.S. 200 mm fab can then make certified companion dies that bond to any compliant array die.
why: Removes periphery NRE (~$50-100M per product) as a barrier for new U.S. entrants and creates interchangeable second-source supply.

title: Sprue-and-runner test periphery: built in scribe lanes, sawn off at dicing
idea: Like the sprues and runners trimmed off a molded part, put test-mode logic, compressed-test comparators, extra probe pads and fuse-programming drivers in the 80-100 um scribe lanes at 180 nm rules, linked across the seal ring by sacrificial connections. After wafer sort and repair, the dicing saw removes them.
why: Recovers the ~3-5% of die area spent on test-only periphery: a direct ~4% bits-per-wafer gain with no process change.
